entries.71338a776acc01c2460f0c4d13036e5b7d135bf1: <div sID="gen4946" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Judg.14" sID="Judg.14"/> <div eID="gen4946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4947" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4948" type="x-p"/> The idea which this chapter gives us of Samson is not what one might have expected concerning one who, by the special designation of heaven, was a Nazarite to God and a deliverer of Israel; and yet really he was both. Here is, I. Samson's courtship of a daughter of the Philistines, and his marriage to her, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.1-Judg.14.5">ver. 1-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.8">8</reference>. II. His conquest of a lion, and the prize he found in the carcase of it, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.5-Judg.14.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.9">9</reference>. III. Samson's riddle proposed to his companions (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.10-Judg.14.14">ver. 10-14</reference>) and unriddled by the treachery of his wife, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.15-Judg.14.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. IV. The occasion this gave him to kill thirty of the Philistines (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.19">ver. 19</reference>) and to break off his new alliance, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.20">ver. 20</reference>.
entries.4869a18c832d6d8683241ca49786fd77f5177d1a: <div eID="gen4948" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4947" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Samson Chooses a Philistine Wife; A Lion Slain by Samson. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1141.)</title> <div sID="gen4949" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Samson went down to Timnath, and saw a woman in Timnath of the daughters of the Philistines. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he came up, and told his father and his mother, and said, I have seen a woman in Timnath of the daughters of the Philistines: now therefore get her for me to wife. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then his father and his mother said unto him, <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren, or among all my people, that thou goest to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines? And Samson said unto his father, Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well. <hi type="super">4</hi> But his father and his mother knew not that it <hi type="italic">was</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he sought an occasion against the Philistines: for at that time the Philistines had dominion over Israel. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then went Samson down, and his father and his mother, to Timnath, and came to the vineyards of Timnath: and, behold, a young lion roared against him. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would have rent a kid, and <hi type="italic">he had</hi> nothing in his hand: but he told not his father or his mother what he had done. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he went down, and talked with the woman; and she pleased Samson well. <hi type="super">8</hi> And after a time he returned to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcase of the lion: and, behold, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a swarm of bees and honey in the carcase of the lion. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he took thereof in his hands, and went on eating, and came to his father and mother, and he gave them, and they did eat: but he told not them that he had taken the honey out of the carcase of the lion. <div eID="gen4949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4950" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Samson, under the extraordinary guidance of Providence, seeks an occasion of quarrelling with the Philistines, by joining in affinity with them—a strange method, but the truth is Samson was himself a riddle, a paradox of a man, did that which was really great and good, by that which was seemingly weak and evil, because he was designed not to be a pattern to us (who must walk by rule, not by example), but a type of him who, though he knew no sin, was made sin for us, and appeared <hi type="italic">in the likeness of sinful flesh,</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">condemn</hi> and <hi type="italic">destroy sin in the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen4950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4951" type="x-p"/> 1. As the negotiation of Samson's marriage was a common case, we may observe, (1.) That is was weakly and foolishly done of him to set his affections upon a daughter of the Philistines; the thing appeared very improper. Shall one that is not only an Israelite, but a Nazarite, devoted to the Lord, covet to become one with a worshipper of Dagon? Shall one marked for a patriot of his country match among those that are its sworn enemies? He saw this woman (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.1">v. 1</reference>), and she <hi type="italic">pleased him well,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.3">v. 3</reference>. It does not appear that he had any reason to think her wise or virtuous, or in any way likely to be a help-meet for him; but he saw something in her face that was very agreeable to his fancy, and therefore nothing will serve but she must be his wife. He that in the choice of a wife is guided only by his eye, and governed by his fancy, must afterwards thank himself if he find a Philistine in his arms. (2.) Yet it was wisely and well done not to proceed so much as to make his addresses to her till he had first made his parents acquainted with the matter. He told them, and desired them to <hi type="italic">get her for him to wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.2">v. 2</reference>. Herein he is an example to all children. Conformably to the law of the fifth commandment, children ought not to marry, nor to move towards marrying, without the advice and consent of their parents; those that do (as bishop Hall here expresses it) <hi type="italic">wilfully unchild themselves, and exchange natural affections for violent.</hi> Parents have a property in their children as parts of themselves. In marriage this property is transferred; for such is the law of the relation that <hi type="italic">a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife.</hi> It is therefore not only unkind and ungrateful, but very unjust, to alienate this property without their concurrence; whoso thus <hi type="italic">robbeth his father or mother,</hi> stealing himself from them, who is nearer and dearer to them than their goods, <hi type="italic">and</hi> yet <hi type="italic">saith, It is no transgression, the same is the companion of a destroyer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.24">Prov. xxviii. 24</reference>. (3.) His parents did well to dissuade him from yoking himself thus unequally with unbelievers. Let those who profess religion, but are courting an affinity with the profane and irreligious, matching into families where they have reason to think the fear of God is not, nor the worship of God, let them hear their reasoning, and apply it to themselves: "<hi type="italic">Is there never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren,</hi> or, if none of our tribe, <hi type="italic">never a one among all thy people,</hi> never an Israelite, that pleases thee, or that thou canst think worthy of thy affection, that thou shouldest marry a Philistine?" In the old world the sons of God corrupted and ruined themselves, their families, and that truly primitive church, by marrying with the <hi type="italic">daughters of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.2">Gen. vi. 2</reference>. God had forbidden the people of Israel to marry with the devoted nations, one of which the Philistines were, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3">Deut. vii. 3</reference>. (4.) If there had not been a special reason for it, it certainly would have been improper in him to insist upon his choice, and in them to agree to it at last. Yet their tender compliance with his affections may be observed as an example to parents not to be unreasonable in crossing their children's choices, nor to deny their consent, especially to those that have seasonably and dutifully asked it, without some very good cause. As children must <hi type="italic">obey their parents in the Lord,</hi> so parents must not <hi type="italic">provoke their children to wrath, lest they be discouraged.</hi> This Nazarite, in his subjection to his parents, asking their consent, and not proceeding till he had it, was not only an example to all children, but a type of the holy child Jesus, who <hi type="italic">went down with his parents to Nazareth</hi> (thence called a <hi type="italic">Nazarene</hi>) and was subject to them, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.51">Luke ii. 51</reference>. <div eID="gen4951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4952" type="x-p"/> 2. But this treaty of marriage is expressly said to be <hi type="italic">of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.4">v. 4</reference>. Not only that God afterwards overruled it to serve his designs against the Philistines, but that he put it into Samson's heart to make this choice, that he <hi type="italic">might have occasion against the Philistine.</hi> It was not a thing evil in itself for him to marry a Philistine. It was forbidden because of the danger of receiving hurt by idolaters; where there was not only no danger of that kind, but an opportunity hoped for of doing that hurt to them which would be good service to Israel, the law might well be dispense with. It was said (<reference osisRef="Judg.13.25">ch. xiii. 25</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord began to move him at times,</hi> and we have reason to think he himself perceived that Spirit to move him at this time, when he made this choice, and that otherwise he would have yielded to his parents' dissuasives, nor would they have consented at last if he had not satisfied them it was <hi type="italic">of the Lord.</hi> This would bring him into acquaintance and converse with the Philistines, by which he might have such opportunities of galling them as otherwise he could not have. It should seem, the way in which the Philistines oppressed Israel was, not by great armies, but by the clandestine incursions of their giants and small parties of their plunderers. In the same way therefore Samson must deal with them; let him but by this marriage get among them, and he would be a <hi type="italic">thorn in their sides.</hi> Jesus Christ, having to deliver us from this present evil world, and to cast out the prince of it, did himself visit it, though full of pollution and enmity, and, by assuming a body, did in some sense join in affinity with it, that he might destroy our spiritual enemies, and his own arm might work the salvation. <div eID="gen4952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4953" type="x-p"/> II. Samson, by a special providence, is animated and encouraged to attack the Philistines. That being the service for which he was designed, God, when he called him to it, prepared him for it by two occurrences:— <div eID="gen4953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4954" type="x-p"/> 1. By enabling him, in one journey to Timnath, to <hi type="italic">kill a lion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.5-Judg.14.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Many decline doing the service they might do because they <hi type="italic">know not their own strength.</hi> God let Samson know what he could do in the strength of the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord,</hi> that he might never be afraid to look the greatest difficulties in the face. David, who was to complete the destruction of the Philistines, must try his hand first upon <hi type="italic">a lion and a bear,</hi> that thence he might infer, as we may suppose Samson did, that the uncircumcised Philistine should be as one of them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.36">1 Sam. xvii. 36</reference>. (1.) Samson's encounter with the lion was hazardous. It was a young lion, one of the fiercest sort, that set upon him, roaring for his prey, and setting his eye particularly upon him; <hi type="italic">he roared in meeting him,</hi> so the word is. He was all alone in the vineyards, whither he had rambled from his father and mother (who kept the high road), probably to eat grapes. Children consider not how they expose themselves to the roaring lion that seeks to devour when, out of a foolish fondness for liberty, they wander from under the eye and wing of their prudent pious parents. Nor do young people consider what lions lurk in the vineyards, the vineyards of red wines, as dangerous as snakes under the green grass. Had Samson met with this lion in the way, he might have had more reason to expect help both from God and man than here in the solitary vineyards, out of his road. But there was a special providence in it, and the more hazardous the encounter was, (2.) The victory was so much the more illustrious. It was obtained without any difficulty: he strangled the lion, and tore his throat as easily as he would have strangled a kid, yet without any instrument, not only no sword nor bow, but not so much as a staff or knife; he had <hi type="italic">nothing in his hand.</hi> Christ engaged the roaring lion, and conquered him in the beginning of his public work (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11">Matt. iv. 1</reference>, &c.), and afterwards spoiled principalities and powers, triumphing over them <hi type="italic">in himself,</hi> as some read it, not by any instrument. He was <hi type="italic">exalted in his own strength.</hi> That which added much to the glory of Samson's triumph over the lion was that when he had done this great exploit he did not boast of it, did <hi type="italic">not so much as tell his father nor mother</hi> that which many a one would soon have published through the whole country. Modesty and humility make up the brightest crown of great performances. <div eID="gen4954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4955" type="x-p"/> 2. By providing him, the next journey, with honey in the carcase of this lion, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.8-Judg.14.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. When he came down the next time to solemnize his nuptials, and his parents with him, he had the curiosity to turn aside into the vineyard where he had killed the lion, perhaps that with the sight of the place he might affect himself with the mercy of that great deliverance, and might there solemnly give thanks to God for it. It is good thus to <hi type="italic">remind ourselves</hi> of God's former favours to us. There he found the carcase of the lion; the birds or beasts of prey, it is likely, had eaten the flesh, and in the skeleton a swarm of bees had knit, and made a hive of it, and had not been idle, but had there laid up a good stock of honey, which was one of the staple commodities of Canaan; such plenty there was of it that the land is said to <hi type="italic">flow with milk and honey.</hi> Samson, having a better title than any man to the hive, seizes the honey with his hands. This supposes an encounter with the bees; but he that dreaded not lion's paws had no reason to fear <hi type="italic">their</hi> stings. As by his victory over the lion he was emboldened to encounter the Philistine-giants, if there should be occasion, notwithstanding their strength and fierceness, so by dislodging the bees he was taught not to fear the multitude of the Philistines; though they <hi type="italic">compassed him about like bees, yet in the name of the Lord he should destroy them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Ps. cxviii. 12</reference>. Of the honey he here found, (1.) He ate himself, asking no questions for conscience' sake; for the dead bones of an unclean beast had not that ceremonial pollution in them that the bones of a man had. John Baptist, that Nazarite of the New Testament, lived upon wild honey. (2.) He gave to his parents, and they did eat; he did not eat all himself. <hi type="italic">Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee,</hi> and no more, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Prov. xxv. 16</reference>. He let his parents share with him. Children should be grateful to their parents with the fruits of their own industry, and so <hi type="italic">show piety at home,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1 Tim. v. 4</reference>. Let those that by the grace of God have found sweetness in religion themselves communicate their experience to their friends and relations, and invite them to come and share with them. He told not his parents whence he had it, lest they should scruple eating it. Bishop Hall observes here that <hi type="italic">those are less wise and more scrupulous than Samson that decline the use of God's gifts because they find them in ill vessels.</hi> Honey is honey still, though in a dead lion. Our Lord Jesus having conquered Satan, that roaring lion, believers find honey in the carcase, abundant strength and satisfaction, enough for themselves and for all their friends, from that victory.
entries.d62f3dac3a97bcee0cfeb402cbd54732bf311582: <div eID="gen4955" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Samson's Riddle; Slaughter of the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1141.)</title> <div sID="gen4956" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> So his father went down unto the woman: and Samson made there a feast; for so used the young men to do. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it came to pass, when they saw him, that they brought thirty companions to be with him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Samson said unto them, I will now put forth a riddle unto you: if ye can certainly declare it me within the seven days of the feast, and find <hi type="italic">it</hi> out, then I will give you thirty sheets and thirty change of garments: <hi type="super">13</hi> But if ye cannot declare <hi type="italic">it</hi> me, then shall ye give me thirty sheets and thirty change of garments. And they said unto him, Put forth thy riddle, that we may hear it. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he said unto them, Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not in three days expound the riddle. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass on the seventh day, that they said unto Samson's wife, Entice thy husband, that he may declare unto us the riddle, lest we burn thee and thy father's house with fire: have ye called us to take that we have? <hi type="italic">is it</hi> not <hi type="italic">so?</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> And Samson's wife wept before him, and said, Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not: thou hast put forth a riddle unto the children of my people, and hast not told <hi type="italic">it</hi> me. And he said unto her, Behold, I have not told <hi type="italic">it</hi> my father nor my mother, and shall I tell <hi type="italic">it</hi> thee? <hi type="super">17</hi> And she wept before him the seven days, while their feast lasted: and it came to pass on the seventh day, that he told her, because she lay sore upon him: and she told the riddle to the children of her people. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the men of the city said unto him on the seventh day before the sun went down, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> sweeter than honey? and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> stronger than a lion? And he said unto them, If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon, and slew thirty men of them, and took their spoil, and gave change of garments unto them which expounded the riddle. And his anger was kindled, and he went up to his father's house. <hi type="super">20</hi> But Samson's wife was <hi type="italic">given</hi> to his companion, whom he had used as his friend. <div eID="gen4956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4957" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Samson's wedding feast and the occasion it gave him to fall foul upon the Philistines. <div eID="gen4957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4958" type="x-p"/> I. Samson conformed to the custom of the country in making a festival of his nuptial solemnities, which continued seven days, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.10">v. 10</reference>. Though he was a Nazarite, he did not affect, in a thing of this nature, to be singular, but did <hi type="italic">as the young men used to do</hi> upon such occasions. It is no part of religion to go contrary to the innocent usages of the places where we live: nay, it is a reproach to religion when those who profess it give just occasion to others to call them covetous, sneaking, and morose. A good man should strive to make himself, in the best sense, a good companion. <div eID="gen4958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4959" type="x-p"/> II. His wife's relations paid him the accustomed respect of the place upon that occasion, and brought him thirty young men to keep him company during the solemnity, and to attend him as his grooms-men (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">When they saw him,</hi> what a comely man he was, and what an ingenuous graceful look he had, they brought him these to do him honour, and to improve by his conversation while he staid among them. Or, rather, when they saw him, what a strong stout man he was, they brought these, seemingly to be his companions, but really to be a guard upon him, or spies to observe him. Jealous enough they were of him, but would have been more so had they known of his victory over the lion, which therefore he had industriously concealed. The favours of Philistines have often some mischief or other designed in them. <div eID="gen4959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4960" type="x-p"/> III. Samson, to entertain the company, propounds a riddle to them, and lays a wager with them that they cannot find it out in seven days, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.12-Judg.14.14">v. 12-14</reference>. The usage, it seems, was very ancient upon such occasions, when friends were together, to be innocently merry, not to spend all the time in dull eating and drinking, as bishop Patrick expresses it, or in other gratifications of sense, as music, dancing, or shows, but to propose questions, by which their learning and ingenuity might be tried and improved. This becomes men, wise men, that value themselves by their reason; but very unlike to it are the infamous and worse than brutish entertainments of this degenerate age, which send nothing round but the glass and the health, till reason is drowned, and wisdom sunk. Now, 1. Samson's riddle was his own invention, for it was his own achievement that gave occasion for it: <hi type="italic">Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness.</hi> Read my riddle, what is this? Beasts of prey do not yield meat for man, yet <hi type="italic">food came from the devourer;</hi> and those creatures that are strong when they are alive commonly smell strong and are every way offensive when they are dead, as horses, and yet <hi type="italic">out of the strong,</hi> or out of <hi type="italic">the bitter,</hi> so the Syriac and Arabic read it, <hi type="italic">came sweetness.</hi> If they had but so much sense as to consider what eater is most strong, and what meat is most sweet, they would have found out the riddle, and neither lions nor honey were such strangers to their country that the thoughts of them needed to be out of the way; and the solving of the riddle would have given him occasion to tell them the entertaining story on which it was founded. This riddle is applicable to many of the methods of divine providence and grace. When God, by an over-ruling providence, brings good out of evil to his church and people,—when that which threatened their ruin turns to their advantage,—when their enemies are made serviceable to them, and the wrath of men turns to God's praise,—then comes <hi type="italic">meat out of the eater</hi> and <hi type="italic">sweetness out of the strong.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Phil. i. 12</reference>. 2. His wager was more considerable to him than to them, because he was one against thirty partners. It was not a wager laid upon God's providence, or upon the chance of a die or a card, but upon their ingenuity, and amounted to no more than an honorary recompence of wit and a disgrace upon stupidity. <div eID="gen4960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4961" type="x-p"/> IV. His companions, when they could not expound the riddle themselves, obliged his wife to get from him the exposition of it, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.15">v. 15</reference>. Whether they were really of a dull capacity, or whether under a particular infatuation at this time, it was strange that none of the thirty could in all this time stumble upon so plain a thing as that, <hi type="italic">What is sweeter than honey</hi> and <hi type="italic">what stronger than a lion?</hi> It should seem that in wit, as well as manners, they were barbarous—barbarous indeed to threaten the bride that, if she would not use means with the bridegroom to let them into the meaning of it, they would <hi type="italic">burn her and her father's house with fire.</hi> Could any thing be more brutish? It was base enough to turn a jest into earnest, and those were unworthy of conversation that would grow so outrageous rather than confess their ignorance and lose so small a wager; nor would it save their credit at all to tell the riddle when they were told it. It was yet more villainous to engage Samson's wife to be a traitor to her own husband, and to pretend a greater interest in her than he had. Now that she was married she must <hi type="italic">forget her own people.</hi> Yet most inhuman of all was it to threaten, if she could not prevail, to burn her and all her relations with fire, and all for fear of losing each of them the value of a shirt and a coat: <hi type="italic">Have you called us to take what we have?</hi> Those must never lay wagers that cannot lose more tamely and easily than thus. <div eID="gen4961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4962" type="x-p"/> V. His wife, by unreasonable importunity, obtains from him a key to his riddle. It was <hi type="italic">on the seventh day,</hi> that is, the seventh day of the week (as Dr. Lightfoot conjectures), but the fourth day of the feast, that they solicited her to entice her husband (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.15">v. 15</reference>), and she did it, 1. With great art and management (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.16">v. 16</reference>), resolving not to believe he loved her, unless he would gratify her in this thing. She knew he could not bear to have his love questioned, and therefore, if any thing would work upon him, that would: "<hi type="italic">Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not,</hi> if thou deniest me;" whereas he had much more reason to say, "Thou dost but <hi type="italic">hate me,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lovest me not,</hi> if thou insistest on it." And, that she might not make this the test of his affection, he assures her he had not told his own parents, notwithstanding the confidence he reposed in them. If this prevail not, she will try the powerful eloquence of tears: she <hi type="italic">wept before him</hi> the rest of <hi type="italic">the days of the feast,</hi> choosing rather to mar the mirth, as the bride's tears must needs do, than not gain her point, and oblige her countrymen, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.17">v. 17</reference>. 2. With great success. At last, being quite wearied with her importunity, he told her what was the meaning of his riddle, and though we may suppose she promised secresy, and that if he would but let her know she would tell nobody, she immediately told it to the <hi type="italic">children of her people;</hi> nor could he expect better from a Philistine, especially when the interests of her country were ever so little concerned. See <reference osisRef="Mic.7.5-Mic.7.6">Mic. vii. 5, 6</reference>. The riddle is at length <hi type="italic">unriddled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is sweeter than honey,</hi> or a better meat? <reference osisRef="Prov.24.13">Prov. xxiv. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">What is stronger than a lion,</hi> or a greater devourer? Samson generously owns they had won the wager, though he had good reason to dispute it, because they had not declared the riddle, as the bargain was (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.12">v. 12</reference>), but it had been declared to them. But he only thought fit to tell them of it: <hi type="italic">If you had not ploughed with my heifer,</hi> made use of your interest with my wife, <hi type="italic">you would not have found out my riddle.</hi> Satan, in his temptations, could not do us the mischief he does if he did not plough with the heifer of our own corrupt nature. <div eID="gen4962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4963" type="x-p"/> VI. Samson pays his wager to these Philistines with the spoils of others of their countrymen, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.19">v. 19</reference>. He took this occasion to quarrel with the Philistines, went down to Ashkelon, one of their cities, where probably he knew there was some great festival observed at this time, to which many flocked, out of whom he picked out thirty, slew them, and took their clothes, and gave them to those that had expounded the riddle; so that, in balancing the account, it appeared that the Philistines were the losers, for one of the lives they lost was worth all the suits of clothes they won: the body is more than raiment. <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord came upon him,</hi> both to authorize and to enable him to do this. <div eID="gen4963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4964" type="x-p"/> VII. This proves a good occasion of weaning Samson from his new relations. He found how his companions had abused him and how his wife had betrayed him, and therefore <hi type="italic">his anger was kindled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.19">v. 19</reference>. Better be angry with Philistines than in love with them, because, when we join ourselves to them, we are most in danger of being ensnared by them. And, meeting with this ill usage among them, he <hi type="italic">went up to his father's house.</hi> It were well for us if the unkindnesses we meet with from the world, and our disappointments in it, had but this good effect upon us, to oblige us by faith and prayer to return to our heavenly Father's house and rest there. The inconveniences that occur in our way should make us love home and long to be there. No sooner had he gone than his wife was disposed of to another, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.20">v. 20</reference>. Instead of begging his pardon for the wrong she had done him, when he justly signified his resentment of it only by withdrawing in displeasure for a time, she immediately marries him that was the chief of the guests, the friend of the bridegroom, whom perhaps she loved too well, and was too willing to oblige, when she got her husband to tell her the riddle. See how little confidence is to be put in man, when those may prove our enemies whom we have used as our friends.  <chapter eID="Judg.14"/> <div eID="gen4964" type="x-p"/>

entries.651be3b20845e99bd64714e50a084140c712435a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2370"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.14.1-Judg.14.5">Jud 14:1-5</reference>. Samson Desires a Wife of the Philistines.</title> <div sID="gen3192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2370"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Timnath--</hi>now Tibna, about three miles from Zorah, his birthplace.<div eID="gen3192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saw a woman ... of the Philistines; and told his father and his mother, and said, ... get her for me to wife--</hi>In the East parents did, and do in many cases still, negotiate the marriage alliances for their sons. During their period of ascendency, the Philistine invaders had settled in the towns; and the intercourse between them and the Israelites was often of such a friendly and familiar character as to issue in matrimonial relations. Moreover, the Philistines were not in the number of the seven devoted nations of Canaan [De 7:1-3]--with whom the law forbade them to marry. <div eID="gen3193" type="x-p"/>
entries.2bafc399f97dbbbc957da8d61059e20d62b917ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2371"/><div sID="gen3194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2371"/><hi type="bold">3-4. Is there never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren--</hi>that is, "of thine own tribe"--a Danite woman.<div eID="gen3194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Samson said ... Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well--</hi>literally, "she is right in mine eyes"; not by her beautiful countenance or handsome figure, but right or fit for his purpose. And this throws light on the historian's remark in reference to the resistance of his parents: they "knew not that it was of the Lord, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines"--rather, "from the Philistines"--originating on their side. The Lord, by a course of retributive proceedings, was about to destroy the Philistine power, and the means which He meant to employ was not the forces of a numerous army, as in the case of the preceding judges, but the miraculous prowess of the single-handed champion of Israel. In these circumstances, the provocation to hostilities could only spring out of a private quarrel, and this marriage scheme was doubtless suggested by the secret influence of the Spirit as the best way of accomplishing the intended result. <div eID="gen3195" type="x-p"/>
entries.94dc19acf3994060651d3dd813219b88563a87cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2372"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.14.5-Judg.14.9">Jud 14:5-9</reference>. He Kills a Lion.</title> <div sID="gen3196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2372"/><hi type="bold">5-9. a young lion--</hi>Hebrew, a lion in the pride of his youthful prime. The wild mountain passes of Judah were the lairs of savage beasts; and most or all the "lions" of Scripture occur in that wild country. His rending and killing the shaggy monster, without any weapon in his hand, were accomplished by that superhuman courage and strength which the occasional influences of the Spirit enabled him to put forth, and by the exertion of which, in such private incidental circumstances, he was gradually trained to confide in them for the more public work to which he was destined. <div eID="gen3196" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1b49932e48dd504110cf398c0785a18639b60d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2375"/><div sID="gen3201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2375"/><hi type="bold">10-11. his father went down--</hi>The father is mentioned as the head and representative of Samson's relatives.<div eID="gen3201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Samson made there a feast--</hi>The wedding festivity lasted a week. The men and women were probably entertained in separate apartments--the bride, with her female relatives, at her parents' house; Samson, in some place obtained for the occasion, as he was a stranger. A large number of paranymphs, or "friends of the bridegroom," furnished, no doubt, by the bride's family, attended his party, ostensibly to honor the nuptials, but really as spies on his proceedings. <div eID="gen3202" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e1136354c985cb5773b959d4ac82c9ec437d814: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2376"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.14.12-Judg.14.18">Jud 14:12-18</reference>. His Riddle.</title> <div sID="gen3203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2376"/><hi type="bold">12-18. I will now put forth a riddle--</hi>Riddles are a favorite Oriental amusement at festive entertainments of this nature, and rewards are offered to those who give the solution. Samson's riddle related to honey in the lion's carcass. The prize he offered was thirty sindinim, or shirts, and thirty changes of garments, probably woolen. Three days were passed in vain attempts to unravel the enigma. The festive week was fast drawing to a close when they secretly enlisted the services of the newly married wife, who having got the secret, revealed it to her friends. <div eID="gen3203" type="x-p"/>
entries.89075eb2863f78035917c20be8c7b1c190372748: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2378"/><div sID="gen3206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2378"/><hi type="bold">19-20. went down to Ashkelon, and slew thirty men of them--</hi>This town was about twenty-four miles west by southwest from Timnah; and his selection of this place, which was dictated by the Divine Spirit, was probably owing to its bitter hostility to Israel.<div eID="gen3206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">took their spoil--</hi>The custom of stripping a slain enemy was unknown in Hebrew warfare. <div eID="gen3207" type="x-p"/>

entries.56e362bb21388d74411b5d7b8fb739a2cde0dcb7: <div eID="gen8932" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8933" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8934" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8934" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8933" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8935" type="x-p"/> Samson marries a wife of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.1-Jdg.14.4">Jdg 14:1-4</reference>. Slays a young lion at Timnath, in the carcass of which he afterwards finds a swarm of bees, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.5-Jdg.14.9">Jdg 14:5-9</reference>. He makes a feast; they appoint him thirty companions, to whom he puts forth a riddle, which they cannot expound, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.10-Jdg.14.14">Jdg 14:10-14</reference>. They entice his wife to get the interpretation from him; she succeeds, informs them, and they tell the explanation, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.15-Jdg.14.18">Jdg 14:15-18</reference>. He is incensed, and slays thirty of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.19">Jdg 14:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.20">Jdg 14:20</reference>. <div eID="gen8935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8936" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8937" type="x-p"/> Went down to Timnath - A frontier town of the Philistines, at the beginning of the lands belonging to the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.57">Jos 15:57</reference>; but afterwards given up to Dan, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference>. David took this place from the Philistines, but they again got possession of it in the reign of Ahaz, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Chr 28:18</reference>.
entries.9af95a5f266a4cb0c14f110742cc7d1a1525b6be: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8938" type="x-p"/> Is there never a woman - To marry with any that did not belong to the Israelitish stock, was contrary to the law, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.16">Exo 34:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.7.3">Deu 7:3</reference>. But this marriage of Samson was said to be of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.4">Jdg 14:4</reference>; that is, God permitted it, (for in no other sense can we understand the phrase), that it might be a means of bringing about the deliverance of Israel. <div eID="gen8938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8939" type="x-p"/> For she pleaseth me well - כי היאישרה בעיני ki hi yisherah beeynai, for she is right in my eyes. This is what is supposed to be a sufficient reason to justify either man or woman in their random choice of wife or husband; the maxim is the same with that of the poet: - "Thou hast no fault, or I no fault can spy; <div eID="gen8939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8940" type="x-p"/> Thou art all beauty or all blindness I." <div eID="gen8940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8941" type="x-p"/> When the will has sufficient power, its determinations are its own rule of right. That will should be pure and well directed that says, It shall be so, because I Will it should be so. A reason of this kind is similar to that which I have seen in a motto on the brass ordnance of Lewis XIV., Ultima Ratio Regum, the sum of regal logic; i.e., "My will, backed by these instruments of destruction, shall be the rule of right and wrong." The rules and principles of this logic are now suspected; and it is not likely to be generally received again without violent demonstration.
entries.4452d21c042964cbf132dc942bed3ea9b0cee1ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen8941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8942" type="x-p"/> A young lion roared against him - Came fiercely out upon him, ready to tear him to pieces.
entries.2faea22d6f0c80f6a7e8a6b82ef6e9ae60f47e95: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen8942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8943" type="x-p"/> He rent him as he would have rent a kid - Now it is not intimated that he did this by his own natural strength, but by the Spirit of the Lord coming mightily upon him: so that his strength does not appear to be his own, nor to be at his command; his might was, by the will of God, attached to his hair and to his Nazarate.
entries.6a33433e5a32b0854cdbf92f4bf5662d0c69f30e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen8943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8944" type="x-p"/> And talked with the woman - That is, concerning marriage; thus forming the espousals.
entries.57d068448a5aee6375948e77544b34e5802c44ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen8944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8945" type="x-p"/> After a time - Probably about one year; as this was the time that generally elapsed between espousing and wedding. <div eID="gen8945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8946" type="x-p"/> A swarm of bees and honey in the carcass - By length of time the flesh had been entirely consumed off the bones, and a swarm of bees had formed their combs within the region of the thorax, nor was it an improper place; nor was the thing unfrequent, if we may credit ancient writers; the carcasses of slain beasts becoming a receptacle for wild bees. The beautiful espisode in the 4th Georgic of Virgil, beginning at ver. 317, proves that the ancients believed that bees might be engendered in the body of a dead ox: - <div eID="gen8946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8947" type="x-p"/> Pastor Aristaeus fugiens Peneia Tempe - <div eID="gen8947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8948" type="x-p"/> Quatuor eximios praestanti corpore tauros <div eID="gen8948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8949" type="x-p"/> Ducit, et intacta totidem cervice juvencas. <div eID="gen8949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8950" type="x-p"/> Post, ubi nona suos Aurora induxerat ortus. <div eID="gen8950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8951" type="x-p"/> Inferias Orphei mittit, lucumque revisit. <div eID="gen8951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8952" type="x-p"/> Hic ver o subitum, ac dietu mirabile monstrum <div eID="gen8952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8953" type="x-p"/> Adspiciunt, liquefacta bourn per viscera toto <div eID="gen8953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8954" type="x-p"/> Stridere apes utero, et ruptis effervere costis; <div eID="gen8954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8955" type="x-p"/> Immensasque trahi nubes, jamque arbore summa <div eID="gen8955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8956" type="x-p"/> Confluere, et lentis uvam demittere ramis. <div eID="gen8956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8957" type="x-p"/> Virg. Geor. lib. iv., ver. 550. "Sad Aristaeus from fair Tempe fled, <div eID="gen8957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8958" type="x-p"/> His bees with famine or diseases dead - <div eID="gen8958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8959" type="x-p"/> Four altars raises, from his herd he culls <div eID="gen8959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8960" type="x-p"/> For slaughter four the fairest of his bulls; <div eID="gen8960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8961" type="x-p"/> Four heifers from his female store he took, <div eID="gen8961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8962" type="x-p"/> All fair, and all unknowing of the yoke. <div eID="gen8962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8963" type="x-p"/> Nine mornings thence, with sacrifice and prayers, <div eID="gen8963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8964" type="x-p"/> The powers atoned, he to the grove repairs. <div eID="gen8964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8965" type="x-p"/> Behold a prodigy! for, from within <div eID="gen8965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8966" type="x-p"/> The broken bowels, and the bloated skin, <div eID="gen8966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8967" type="x-p"/> A buzzing noise of bees his ears alarms, <div eID="gen8967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8968" type="x-p"/> Straight issuing through the sides assembling swarms! <div eID="gen8968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8969" type="x-p"/> Dark as a cloud, they make a wheeling flight, <div eID="gen8969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8970" type="x-p"/> Then on a neighboring tree descending light, <div eID="gen8970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8971" type="x-p"/> Like a large cluster of black grapes they show, <div eID="gen8971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8972" type="x-p"/> And make a large dependance from the bough. <div eID="gen8972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8973" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.2e70e106f3989afadc621463cbd83b0ea2565f49: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen8973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8974" type="x-p"/> Samson made there a feast - The marriage feast, when he went to marry his espoused wife.
entries.31fb1800d09d5f4506a5bfeff7532187df4562c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen8974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8975" type="x-p"/> They brought thirty companions - These are called in Scripture children of the bride-chamber, and friends of the bridegroom. See the whole of this subject particularly illustrated in the observations at the end of <reference osisRef="Joh.3.25">Joh 3:25</reference> (note).
entries.47855e753cdb6180e74a660511207df93387ca9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen8975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8976" type="x-p"/> I will now put forth a riddle - Probably this was one part of the amusements at a marriage-feast; each in his turn proposing a riddle, to be solved by any of the rest on a particular forfeit; the proposer forfeiting, if solved, the same which the company must forfeit if they could not solve it. <div eID="gen8976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8977" type="x-p"/> Thirty sheets - I have no doubt that the Arab hayk, or hake, is here meant; a dress in which the natives of the East wrap themselves, as a Scottish Highlander does in his plaid. In Asiatic countries the dress scarcely ever changes; being nearly the same now that it was 2000 years ago. Mr. Jackson, in his account of the Empire of Morocco, thus mentions the Moorish dress: "It resembles," says he, "that of the ancient patriarchs, as represented in paintings; (but the paintings are taken from Asiatic models); that of the men consists of a red cap and turban, a (kumja) shirt, which hangs outside of the drawers, and comes down below the knee; a (caftan) coat, which buttons close before, and down to the bottom, with large open sleeves; over which, when they go out of doors, they throw carelessly, and sometimes elegantly, a hayk, or garment of white cotton, silk, or wool, five or six yards long, and five feet wide. The Arabs often dispense with the caftan, and even with the shirt, wearing nothing but the hayk." When an Arab does not choose to wrap himself in the hayk, he throws it over his left shoulder, where it hangs till the weather, etc., obliges him to wrap it round him. The hayk is either mean or elegant, according to the quality of the cloth, and of the person who wears it. I have myself seen the natives of Fez, with hayks, or hykes, both elegant and costly. By the changes of garments, it is very likely that the kumja and caftan are meant, or at least the caftan; but most likely both: for the Hebrew has חליפות בגדים chaliphoth begadim, changes or succession of garments. Samson, therefore, engaged to give or receive thirty hayks, and thirty kumjas and caftans, on the issue of the interpretation or non-interpretation of his riddle: these were complete suits.
entries.038cc037770d1cb7f20c4fad15a61e8f3ddf0d2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8978" type="x-p"/> And he said unto there - Thus he states or proposes his riddle: - <div eID="gen8978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8979" type="x-p"/> Out of the eater came forth meat, <div eID="gen8979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8980" type="x-p"/> And out of the strong came forth sweetness. <div eID="gen8980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8981" type="x-p"/> Instead of strong, the Syriac and Arabic have bitter. I have no doubt that the riddle was in poetry; and perhaps the two hemistichs above preserve its order. This was scarcely a fair riddle; for unless the fact to which it refers were known, there is no rule of interpretation by which it could be found out. We learn from the Scholiast, on Aristophanes, Vesp. v. 20, that it was a custom among the ancient Greeks to propose at their festivals, what were called γριφοι, griphoi, riddles, enigmas, or very obscure sayings, both curious and difficult, and to give a recompense to those who found them out, which generally consisted in either a festive crown, or a goblet full of wine. Those who failed to solve them were condemned to drink a large portion of fresh water, or of wine mingled with a sea-water, which they were compelled to take down at one draught, without drawing their breath, their hands being tied behind their backs. Sometimes they gave the crown to the deity in honor of whom the festival was made: and if none could solve the riddle, the reward was given to him who proposed it. Of these enigmas proposed at entertainments etc., we have numerous examples in Athenaeus, Deipnosoph, lib. x., c. 15, p. 142, edit. Argentorat., and some of them very like this of Samson for example: - Διδους τις ουκ εδωκεν, ουδ' εχων εχει; "Who gives, and does not give? <div eID="gen8981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8982" type="x-p"/> Who has not, and yet has?" <div eID="gen8982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8983" type="x-p"/> This may be spoken of an enigma and its proposer: he gives it, but he does not give the sense; the other has it, but has not the meaning. Εστι φυσις θηλεια βρεφη σοζους' ὑπο κολποις Αυτης· ταυτα δ' αφωνα βοην ἱστησι γεγωνον. Και δια ποντιον οιδμα, και ηπειρου δια πασης, Οἱς εθελει θνητων· τοις δ' ου παρεουσις ακουειν Εξεστι· κωφην δ' ακοης αισθησιν εχουσιν. "There is a feminine Nature, fostering her children in her bosom; who, although they are dumb, send forth a distinct voice over every nation of the earth, and every sea, to whom soever they please. It is possible for those who are absent to hear, and for those who are deaf to hear also." <div eID="gen8983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8984" type="x-p"/> The relator brings in Sappho interpreting it thus: - Θηλεια μεν ουν εστι φυσις, επιστολη. Βρεφη δ' εν αυτῃ περιφερει τα γραμματα Αφωνα δ' οντα ταυτα τοις πορῥω λαλει, Οἱς βουλεθ\uu903? ἑτερος δ' αν τυχῃ τις πλησιον Ἑστως αναγινωσκοντος, ουκ ακουσεται. "The Nature, which is feminine, signifies an epistle; and her children whom she bears are alphabetical characters: and these, being dumb, speak and give counsel to any, even at a distance; though he who stands nigh to him who is silently reading, hears no voice." <div eID="gen8984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8985" type="x-p"/> Here is another, attributed by the same author to Theodectes: - Της φυσεως ὁσα γαια φερει τροφος, ουδ' ὁσα ποντος, Ουτε βροτοισιν εχει γυιων αυξησιν ὁμοιαν. Αλλ' εν μεν γενεσει πρωτοσπορῳ εστι μεγιστη, Εν δε μεσαις ακμαις μικρα, γηρᾳ δε προς αυτῳ Μορφῃ και μεγεθει μειζων παλιν εστιν ἁπαντων. "Neither does the nourishing earth so bear by nature, nor the sea, nor is there among mortals a like increase of parts; for at the period of its birth it is greatest, but in its middle age it is small, and in its old age it is again greater in form and size than all." <div eID="gen8985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8986" type="x-p"/> This is spoken of a shadow. At the rising of the sun in the east, the shadow of an object is projected illimitably across the earth towards the west; at noon, if the sun be vertical to that place, the shadow of the object is entirely lost; at sunsetting, the shadow is projected towards the east, as it was in the morning towards the west. <div eID="gen8986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8987" type="x-p"/> Here is another, from the same author: - Εισι κασιγνηται διτται, ὡν ἡ μια τικτει Την ἑπεραν, αυτη δε τεκους' ὑπο τησδε τεκνουται. "There are two sisters, the one of whom begets the other, and she who is begotten produces her who begat her." <div eID="gen8987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8988" type="x-p"/> Day and night solve this enigma. <div eID="gen8988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8989" type="x-p"/> The following I have taken from Theognis: - Ηδη γαρ με κεκληκε θαλαττιος οικαδε νεκρος, Τεθνηκως, ζωῳ φθεγγομενος στοματι. <div eID="gen8989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8990" type="x-p"/> Theogn. Gnom., in fine. "A dead seaman calls me to his house; And, although he be dead, he speaks with a living mouth." <div eID="gen8990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8991" type="x-p"/> This dead seaman is a conch or large shellfish, of which the poet was about to eat. The mouth by which it spoke signifies its being used as a horn; as it is well known to produce, when opened at the spiral end and blown, a very powerful sound.
entries.bc8e85826b88d92277117e26ef4fe6c480f2c819: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen8991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8992" type="x-p"/> And she wept before him - Not through any love to him, for it appears she had none, but to oblige her paramours; and of this he soon had ample proof.
entries.2701a189d3a192ff5755d78ed968e6323dbb2636: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen8992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8993" type="x-p"/> If ye had not ploughed with my heifer - If my wife had not been unfaithful to my bed, she would not have been unfaithful to my secret; and, you being her paramours, your interest was more precious to her than that of her husband. She has betrayed me through her attachment to you. Calmet has properly remarked, in quoting the Septuagint, that to plough with one's heifer, or to plough in another man's ground, are delicate turns of expression used both by the Greeks and Latins, as well as the Hebrews, to point out a wife's infidelities. Thus Theognis, Gnom. v. 581: - Εχθαιρω δε γυναικα περιδρομον, ανδρα τε μαργον. Ὁς την αλλονριην βουλετ' αρουραν αρουν. "I detest a woman who gads about, and also a libidinous man, who wishes to plough in another man's ground." <div eID="gen8993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8994" type="x-p"/> Fundum alienium arat, incultum familiarem deserit. <div eID="gen8994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8995" type="x-p"/> Plautus. "He ploughs another's farm, and leaves his own heritage uncultivated." <div eID="gen8995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8996" type="x-p"/> Milo domi non est, perepre at Milone profecto <div eID="gen8996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8997" type="x-p"/> Arva vacant, uxor non minus inde parit. <div eID="gen8997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8998" type="x-p"/> Martial. "Milo is not at home, and Milo being from home, his field lies uncultivated; his wife, nevertheless, continues to breed, and brings forth children." <div eID="gen8998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8999" type="x-p"/> There is the same metaphor in the following lines of Virgil: - <div eID="gen8999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9000" type="x-p"/> Hoc faciunt, nimo ne luxu obtusior usus, <div eID="gen9000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9001" type="x-p"/> Sit genitali arvo, sulcosque oblimet inertes. <div eID="gen9001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9002" type="x-p"/> Geor. l. iii., v. 135. <div eID="gen9002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9003" type="x-p"/> In this sense Samson's words were understood by the Septuagint, by the Syriac, and by Rabbi Levi. See Bochart, Hierozoic. p. 1, lib. ii., cap. 41, col. 406. The metaphor was a common one, and we need seek for no other interpretation of the words of Samson.
entries.a3aded3dcc30385321d2aa2271b545d0c59dec4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen9003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9004" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of the Lord came upon him - "The spirit of fortitude from before the Lord." - Targum. He was inspired with unusual courage, and he felt strength proportioned to his wishes. <div eID="gen9004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9005" type="x-p"/> He - slew thirty men - and took their spoils - He took their hayks, their kumjas, and caftans, and gave them to the thirty persons who, by unfair means, had solved his riddle; thus they had what our version calls thirty sheets, and thirty changes of raiment. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.12">Jdg 14:12</reference>.
entries.44f41ed4831b4bc86d86e46afa187a341b38a8d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen9005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9006" type="x-p"/> But Samson's wife was given to his companion - This was the same kind of person who is called the friend of the bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>. And it is very likely that she loved this person better than she loved her husband, and went to him as soon as Samson had gone to his father's house at Zorah. She might, however, have thought herself abandoned by him, and therefore took another; this appears to have been the persuasion of her father, <reference osisRef="Jdg.15.2">Jdg 15:2</reference>. But her betraying his secret and his interests to his enemies was a full proof he was not very dear to her; though, to persuade him to the contrary, she shed many crocodile tears; see <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.16">Jdg 14:16</reference>. He could not keep his own secret, and he was fool enough to suppose that another would be more faithful to him than he was to himself. Multitudes complain of the treachery of friends betraying their secrets, etc., never considering that they themselves have been their first betrayers, in confiding to others what they pretend to wish should be a secret to the whole world! If a man never let his secret out of his own bosom, it is impossible that he should ever be betrayed.  <chapter eID="Judg.14"/> <div eID="gen9006" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f402c921b9b31989a1c263f3122f65a5548a5e0: Jdg 14:1-2 <div eID="gen3404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3405" type="x-p"/> Samson’s First Transactions with the Philistines. - Jdg 14:1-9. At Tibnath, the present <hi type="italic">Tibne</hi>, an hour’s journey to the south-west of Sur'a (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>), to which Samson had gone down from Zorea or Mahaneh-dan, he saw a daughter of the Philistines who pleased him; and on his return he asked his parents to take her for him as a wife (לקח, to take, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.9">Exo 21:9</reference>).
entries.fe35cbe18e1e3911f125f83c9c56ad7e19ec1b78: Jdg 14:3-4 <div eID="gen3405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3406" type="x-p"/> His parents expressed their astonishment at the choice, and asked him whether there was not a woman among the daughters of his brethren (i.e., the members of his own tribe), or among all his people, that he should want to fetch one from the Philistines, the uncircumcised. But Samson repeated his request, because the daughter of the Philistines pleased him. The aversion of his parents to the marriage was well founded, as such a marriage was not in accordance with the law. It is true that the only marriages expressly prohibited in <reference osisRef="Exod.34.16">Exo 34:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3-Deut.7.4">Deu 7:3-4</reference>, are marriages with Canaanitish women; but the reason assigned for this prohibition was equally applicable to marriages with daughters of the Philistines. In fact, the Philistines are reckoned among the Canaanites in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference> upon the very same ground. But Samson was acting under a higher impulse, whereas his parents did not know that it was from Jehovah, i.e., that Jehovah had so planned it; “<hi type="italic">for Samson was seeking an opportunity on account of the Philistines,</hi>” i.e., an occasion to quarrel with them, because, as is afterwards added in the form of an explanatory circumstantial clause, the Philistines had dominion over Israel at that time. תּאנה, ἁπ. λεγ., an opportunity (cf. התאנּה,   2Ki 5:7).
entries.134eee5069ef6a799101721972498628510760c0: Jdg 14:5-6 <div eID="gen3406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3407" type="x-p"/> When Samson went down with his parents to Timnath, a young lion came roaring towards him at the vineyards of that town. Then the Spirit of Jehovah came upon him, so that he tore the lion in pieces as a kid is torn (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “like the tearing in pieces of the kid”), although he had nothing, i.e., no weapon, in his hand. David, when a shepherd, and the hero Benaiah, also slew lions (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.35">1Sa 17:34-35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2Sa 23:20</reference>); and even at the present day Arabs sometimes kill lions with a staff (see <hi type="italic">Winer</hi>, Bibl. R. W. Art. Löwe). Samson’s supernatural strength, the effect of the Spirit of Jehovah, which came upon him, was simply manifested in the fact that he tore the lion in pieces without any weapon whatever in his hand. But he said nothing about it to his parents, who were not eyewitnesses of the deed. This remark is introduced in connection with what follows.
entries.17b276021da40e8f9c0a59f854bb5e47b3be4c02: Jdg 14:7 <div eID="gen3407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3408" type="x-p"/> When he came to Timnath he talked with the girl, and she pleased him. He had only <hi type="italic">seen</hi> her before (Jdg 14:1); but now that his parents had asked for her, he talked with her, and found the first impression that he had received of her fully confirmed.
entries.48aeaf91044f559409ee0a5e04fb611d68afca4c: Jdg 14:8 <div eID="gen3408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3409" type="x-p"/> When some time had elapsed after the betrothal, he came again to fetch her (take her home, marry her), accompanied, as we learn from Jdg 14:9, by his parents. On the way “<hi type="italic">he turned aside</hi> (from the road) <hi type="italic">to see the carcase of the lion; and behold a swarm of bees was in the body of the lion, also honey.</hi>” The word מפּלת, which only occurs here, is derived from נפל, like πτῶμα from πίπτω, and is synonymous with נבלה, <hi type="italic">cadaver</hi>, and signifies not the mere skeleton, as bees would not form their hive in such a place, but the carcase of the lion, which had been thoroughly dried up by the heat of the sun, without passing into a state of putrefaction. “In the desert of Arabia the heat of a sultry season will often dry up all the moisture of men or camels that have fallen dead, within twenty-four hours of their decease, without their passing into a state of decomposition and putrefaction, so that they remain for a long time like mummies, without change and without stench” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>, Bibl. Althk. iv. 2, p. 424). In a carcase dried up in this way, a swarm of bees might form their hive, just as well as in the hollow trunks of trees, or clefts in the rock, or where wild bees are accustomed to form them, notwithstanding the fact that bees avoid both dead bodies and carrion (see <hi type="italic">Bochart, Hieroz, ed. Ros</hi>. iii. p. 355).
entries.fc3be7923ace258a9aacb7e9c749592b4535d379: Jdg 14:9 <div eID="gen3409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3410" type="x-p"/> Samson took it (the honey) in his hands, ate some of it as he went, and also gave some to his father and mother to eat, but did not tell them that he had got the honey out of the dead body of the lion; for in that case they would not only have refused to eat it as being unclean, but would have been aware of the fact, which Samson afterwards took as the subject of the riddle that he proposed to the Philistines. רדה, to tread, to tread down; hence to get forcible possession of, not to break or to take out, neither of which meanings can be established. The combination of רדה and אל־כּפּיו is a pregnant construction, signifying to obtain possession of and take into the hands.<hi type="italic">Samson’s Wedding and Riddle</hi>. - Jdg 14:10. When his father had come down to the girl (sc., to keep the wedding, not merely to make the necessary preparations for his marriage), Samson prepared for a feast there (in Timnath), according to the usual custom (for so used the young men to do).
entries.cf3428b23abcc1d57a1ebf41303877f994855256: Jdg 14:11 <div eID="gen3410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3411" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And when they saw him, they fetched thirty friends, and they were with him</hi>.” The parents or relations of the bride are the subject of the first clause. They invited thirty of their friends in Timnath to the marriage feast, as “children of the bride-chamber” (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">Mat 9:15</reference>), since Samson had not brought any with him. The reading כּראותם from ראה needs no alteration, though <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> would read כּראתם daer from ירא, in accordance with the rendering of the lxx (<hi type="italic">Cod. Al</hi>.) and <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi>, ἐν τῷ φοβεῖσθαι αὐτούς. Fear of Samson would neither be in harmony with the facts themselves, nor with the words אתּו ויּהיוּ, “<hi type="italic">they were with him,</hi>” which it is felt to be necessary to paraphrase in the most arbitrary manner “they watched him.”
entries.21b89fe949688b43b2688a6ae644c26dc832d3b0: Jdg 14:12-14 <div eID="gen3411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3412" type="x-p"/> At the wedding feast Samson said to the guests, “<hi type="italic">I will give you a riddle. If you show it to me during the seven days of the meal </hi>(the wedding festival), <hi type="italic">and guess it, I will give you thirty sedinim</hi> (σινδόνες, <hi type="italic">tunicae</hi>, i.e., clothes worn next to the skin) <hi type="italic">and thirty changes of garments</hi> (costly dresses, that were frequently changed: see at <reference osisRef="Gen.45.22">Gen 45:22</reference>); <hi type="italic">but if ye cannot show it to me, ye shall give me the same number of garments.</hi>” The custom or proposing riddles at banquets by way of entertainment is also to be met with among the ancient Grecians. (For proofs from <hi type="italic">Athenaeus, Pollux, Gellius,</hi> see <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, Hieroz. P. ii. l. ii. c. 12; and <hi type="italic">K. O. Müller</hi>, Dorier, ii. p. 392). As the guests consented to this proposal, Samson gave them the following riddle (Jdg 14:14): “<hi type="italic">Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness.</hi>” This riddle they could not show, i.e., solve, for three days. That is to say, they occupied themselves for three days in trying to find the solution; after that they let the matter rest until the appointed term was drawing near.
entries.1646a8c92b5e4dd6697fbb7e8de4809b4f67f3ec: Jdg 14:15-16 <div eID="gen3412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3413" type="x-p"/> On the seventh day they said to Samson’s wife, “<hi type="italic">Persuade thy husband to show us the riddle,</hi>” sc., through thee, without his noticing it, “<hi type="italic">lest we burn thee and thy father’s house with fire. Have ye invited us to make us poor; is it not so?</hi>” In this threat the barbarism and covetousness of the Philistines came openly to light. הלירשׁנוּ without <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> in the י is the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of ירשׁ, to make poor-a meaning derived from inheriting, not the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of ירשׁ = רוּשׁ, to be poor. הלא, <hi type="italic">nonne</hi>, strengthens the interrogative clause, and has not the signification “here” = הלם. Samson’s wife, however, wept over him, i.e., urged him with tears in her eyes, and said, “<hi type="italic">Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not; thou hast put forth a riddle unto the children of my people</hi> (my countrymen), <hi type="italic">and hast not shown it to me</hi>.” חדתּה is from חוּד. Samson replied, that he had not even shown it to his father and mother, “<hi type="italic">and shall I show it to thee?</hi>”
entries.9e163b141ce65509dc34aab918b4e996e1bf05a5: Jdg 14:17 <div eID="gen3413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3414" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Thus his wife wept before him the seven days of the banquet.</hi>” This statement is not at variance with that in Jdg 14:15, to the effect that it was only on the seventh day that the Philistine young men urged her with threats to entice Samson to tell the riddle, but may be explained very simply in the following manner. The woman had already come to Samson every day with her entreaties from simple curiosity; but Samson resisted them until the seventh day, when she became more urgent than ever, in consequence of this threat on the part of the Philistines. And “<hi type="italic">Samson showed it to her, because she lay sore upon him;</hi>” whereupon she immediately betrayed it to her countrymen.
entries.8bd3043b6f89c81d3ec62e4cf37ca29f54503ce0: Jdg 14:18 <div eID="gen3414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3415" type="x-p"/> Thus on the seventh day, before the sun went down (חרסה = חרס, Jdg 8:13; <reference osisRef="Job.9.7">Job 9:7</reference>, with a toneless <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, a softening down of the feminine termination: see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §173, <hi type="italic">h</hi>.), the men of the city (i.e., the thirty young men who had been invited) said to Samson, “What is sweeter than honey, and what stronger than a lion?” But Samson saw through the whole thing, and replied, “<hi type="italic">If ye had not ploughed with my heifer, ye had not hit upon</hi> (guessed) <hi type="italic">my riddle,</hi>”-a proverbial saying, the meaning of which is perfectly clear.
entries.7b51e0cfa9802653e1717f7b7b78f4c7085dea62: Jdg 14:19 <div eID="gen3415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3416" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless he was obliged to keep his promise (Jdg 14:12). Then the Spirit of Jehovah came upon him. He went down to Ashkelon, slew thirty men of them, i.e., of the Ashkelonites, took their clothes (חליצות, <hi type="italic">exuviae</hi>: see <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.21">2Sa 2:21</reference>), and gave the changes of garments to those who had shown the riddle. This act is described as the operation of the Spirit of Jehovah which came upon Samson, because it showed to the Philistines the superior power of the servants of Jehovah. It was not carnal revenge that had impelled Samson to the deed. It was not till the deed itself was done that his anger was kindled; and even then it was not against the Philistines, to whom he had been obliged to pay or give the thirty garments, but against his wife, who had betrayed his secret to her countrymen, so that he returned to his father’s house, viz., without his wife.
entries.5bad21151d85589407c65b77c82563b284896922: Jdg 14:20 <div eID="gen3416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3417" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And Samson’s wife was given to his friend, whom he had chosen as a friend</hi>.” מרע is not doubt to be understood here in the sense of “the friend of the bridegroom” (Joh 3:29), ὁ νυμφαγωγός (lxx), the conductor of the bride-namely, one of the thirty companions (Jdg 14:10), whom Samson had entrusted with this office at the marriage festival. The faithlessness of the Philistines towards the Israelites was no doubt apparent here; for even if Samson went home enraged at the treacherous behaviour of his wife, without taking her with him, he did not intend to break the marriage tie, as Jdg 15:1-2 clearly shows. So that instead of looking at the wrong by which Samson felt himself aggrieved, and trying to mitigate his wrath, the parents of the woman made the breach irreparable by giving their daughter as a wife to his companion.  <chapter eID="Judg.14"/> <div eID="gen3417" type="x-p"/>

entries.b404fee5e7ab4605ab95d99a97140dea2cc83da5:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="14" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND Samson went down <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">After he was come to mature Age.</ns0:note> to Timnath <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A Place not far from the Sea, of which see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 38. 12. <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 15. 57. and 19. 43.</ns0:note>, and saw a woman in Timnath, of the daugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters of the Philistines.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:204" />2 And he came up, and told his father and his mother, and said, I have seen a woman in Tim<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nath, of the daughters of the Philistines: now there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore get her for me to wife.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then his father and his mother said unto him, <ns0:hi>Is there</ns0:hi> never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren, or among all my people, that thou go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">With whom the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were forbidden to Marry, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 34. 12, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And although the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> were not <ns0:hi>Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naanites</ns0:hi> in their Original, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 10. 14. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 2. 23. yet they were so in their Habitation, and concurrence with them in wickedness, and therefore were liable to the same censures and judgments with them.</ns0:note>? and Samson said unto his Father, Get her for me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This action of <ns0:hi>Sampson</ns0:hi>'s, though against common rules, seems to be warranted, partly by the greatness and goodness of his Design in it; and principally by the instinct and direction of God, which is mentioned in the following words, which was known to <ns0:hi>Sampson,</ns0:hi> but not to his Parents.</ns0:note>; for <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> she is right in mine eyes.</ns0:note> she pleaseth me well <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Not so much for her Beauty, as for the De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign mentioned in the next Verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 But his father and his mother <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 12. 15 2 Chron. 10. 15 and 22. 7. and 25. 20.</ns0:note> knew not that <ns0:hi>it was</ns0:hi> of the LORD, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which he knew by very probable conjecture, if not by particular Inspiration, that Marriage would give him many ways.</ns0:note>: for at that time the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines had dominion over Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Then went Samson down, and his father and his mother <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Who accompanied him, either because they were now acquainted with his Design; or to order the circumstances of that action which they saw he was set upon: or to watch if they could find any occasion to take him off from his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tention.</ns0:note> to Timnath, and came to the vine<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />yards of Timnath <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Whither he had turned aside either by a Divine impulse, or upon some real or pretended occasion.</ns0:note>: and behold, a young lion roared <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in meet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing him.</ns0:note> against him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And the spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Stirred up and increased his courage and bodily strength.</ns0:note>, and he rent him as he would have rent a kid <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">As soon and as safely.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>he had</ns0:hi> nothing in his hand: but he told not his father or his mother what he had done <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Lest by their means it should be publickly known; for he wisely considered, that it was not yet a fit time to awaken the jealousies and fears of the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines concerning him, as this would have done.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
